notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes on 1 Kings 7:1–26, but there are real gaps. I hit my tool limits, so I couldn't read Ellicott's or the Pulpit Commentary on 1 Kings 7, the NET Bible notes, or any Catholic or Orthodox commentary. The Precept Austin page also cut off partway through the House of the Forest of Lebanon section. I found almost nothing specific for vv. 3–6, 9–11 or 16–20, and nothing at all on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage.

**v. 1 (13 years on the palace)**
- **Reading 1: Solomon's priorities had slipped.** David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes the temple took 7 years and the palace 13, and says it seems that Solomon wanted a house that was more glorious than the temple. He quotes G. Campbell Morgan to the same effect. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-7/
- Ligonier (Reformed), as quoted by Precept Austin, says Solomon cared more about the size and detail of his palace than about the sanctuary. It adds that only Christ's atonement covers our own failures to put God first. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-7-commentary
- Chuck Smith says the verse shows where Solomon's priorities began to turn. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-23.html
- **Reading 2: this is unfair to Solomon.** Precept Austin gives three reasons:
  - the palace was really several public and private buildings;
  - David had already planned and supplied the temple, which sped it up;
  - the chapter spends far more words on the temple than on the palace.
  
  It also quotes Alfred Hoerth, who calls the criticism "hardly valid" because God was pleased with the temple, and Dale Ralph Davis, who thinks the writer deliberately plays down the palace. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-7-commentary
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says the palace took longer because no previous building preparations had been made for the palace as for the temple, and there was less urgency about the king's house. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-kings-7.html
- Trapp adds that Solomon had three houses to build in those years. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/1-kings-7.html
- Constable says the complex took longer simply because it was much larger. He adds that Ancient Near Eastern people did not count a king as truly established until he had built a palace. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-7.html
- None of this splits along denominational lines. It is a divide among evangelical teachers.

**vv. 2–5 (House of the Forest of Lebanon)**
- Guzik: so much Lebanese cedar was used that walking inside was like walking in a forest. He links 1 Kings 10:16–17 (gold shields hung there) and Isaiah 22:8, which calls it an armory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-7/
- R. D. Patterson says its exact use is unclear, but Isaiah 22:8 shows it was at least partly an armory. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-7-commentary
- Constable quotes a writer who saw it as an audience chamber or throne hall. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-7.html
- v. 4 (windows): Grant reads the windows as a picture: government looks outward to the people's welfare, while the windowless temple speaks only of God's glory. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/1-kings-7.html

**v. 7 (Hall of Justice)**
- The Homiletical Commentary draws the lesson That the administration of justice is an essential part of good government. It links the hall to the old custom of judging at the city gate. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-kings-7.html

**v. 8 (Pharaoh's daughter)**
- The Homiletical Commentary thinks her house was probably a rear part of the king's house, though complete in itself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-kings-7.html
- Bridgeway calls it a separate palace for the queen. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-8.html

**vv. 9–12 (stonework and courtyard)**
- Smith works out the foundation stones (v. 10) at about 12–15 feet long. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-8.html
- Guzik on v. 12: the palace shared features with the temple, which leaves the impression the palace was better. He applies Haggai 1:3–10. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-7/
- R. D. Patterson on v. 12: enclosing palace and temple together showed that the king acted for God. In this he was a type (an advance picture) of Christ, the Son of David. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64360/

**vv. 13–14 (Huram)**
- He is not King Hiram but a different man, a metalworker (Clarke, Coffman). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-13.html
- Guzik: half Israelite, half Gentile, and the best craftsman available. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-7/
- Matthew Henry: he had by his mother's side an Israelite, of the tribe of Naphtali, by his father's side a man of Tyre. Henry adds that God uses people's ordinary gifts for his service. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-23.html
- **Naphtali here, Dan in 2 Chronicles 2:14.** The commentators reconcile it in several ways:
  - **Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** she was a Danite by birth whose first husband was from Naphtali.
  - **Matthew Poole:** the king of Tyre, who says "Dan," may simply have been mistaken.
  - **Gill:** she may have come from the city of Dan, which lay in Naphtali's territory.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-14.htm
- John MacArthur: one verse probably gives her birthplace, the other where she lived. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-7-commentary
- Patterson: being a widow's son was a real handicap in that world, so his success shows diligence and God's grace. Same URL.
- Bridgeway, by contrast, faults Solomon for hiring a Tyrian with no apparent concern for the wrong religious ideas this man may have had. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-23.html

**vv. 15–20 (pillars and capitals)**
- Poole: the pillars were placed for mere ornament and magnificence, for they supported nothing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-21.htm
- Constable: paired pillars flanked temple entrances across the ancient Near East. Some held up roofs, but these were probably freestanding. The lilies and pomegranates likely stood for the fruitfulness of God's blessing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-23.html
- Bible Hub's study notes link the pomegranates to the pomegranates on the priest's robe (Exodus 28:33–34) and the lilies to purity. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_kings/7.htm

**v. 21 (Jachin and Boaz)**
- **The names:** "he shall establish" and "in it/him is strength." Barnes reads them together as probably "God will establish in strength." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/7-21.htm
- **Conditional promise:** Poole says the pillars stood for God's strength to defend his temple and people, if they were careful to keep the conditions required by God on their parts. Same URL.
- **Spiritual kingdom:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the strength meant was less the stone temple's, since the pillars were destroyed with it, than that of God's spiritual kingdom. Same URL.
- **Gill:** to the worshipper afraid of falling away, Jachin says God will establish him and Boaz points him to Christ as his strength. Same URL.
- **Guzik:** the pillars put worshippers in the right frame of mind. He quotes Patterson and Austel that each king was meant to see he ruled by God's appointment and grace. Some also link the pair to the pillars of cloud and fire. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-7/
- **Covenant reading:** Constable reports Jones's view that they stood for the covenant, especially with David's line. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-23.html
- **Early Jewish and Christian readings** (second-hand, from a Bible Hub article): the Talmud links Jachin with the priesthood and Boaz with the kingship. Origen and Ambrose are said to have seen the pillars as the apostles. https://biblehub.com/q/Jachin_and_Boaz_s_significance_2.htm
- **Fringe use:** Chuck Smith says no one really knows their purpose, and warns that Freemasons and "many Christian mystics make a lot out of" them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-23.html

**v. 23 (the Sea, and "pi = 3")**
- Barnes: the Sea replaced the tabernacle laver for the priests' washing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-23.html
- Gill: it was also a place where priests could dip. Same URL.
- **The 10-across, 30-around problem:**
  - Coffman: round numbers, and only a nit-picker could criticize them.
  - Gill: a round number is given, not an exact mathematical one.
  - Gill's modern editor offers two fixes: the 30 cubits measured the inside while the 10 included the rim, or the 10 measured a flared, cup-like brim (v. 26).
  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-23.html
- Catholic.com: ancient measurements were approximate, and a writer would simply have rounded 9.55 up to 10. https://www.catholic.com/audio/ddp/the-bible-and-pi

**v. 24 (buds under the rim)**
- Constable: symbols of fertility decorated it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-23.html

**v. 25 (twelve oxen)**
- Guzik: the oxen represented the twelve tribes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-7/
- Constable: either the 12 tribes or Solomon's 12 districts. He also calls them symbols of strength and service. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-23.html
- **Was making them wrong?** Coffman (Churches of Christ) says the oxen broke the commandment against graven images. He cites Josephus, who said Solomon sinned in this. He rejects Whiston's defence that Solomon followed a God-given pattern from David. Same URL.

**v. 26 (2,000 baths here, 3,000 in 2 Chronicles 4:5)**
- **Normal level vs. full capacity:** Wiersbe, Barnes and Constable all say 3,000 was the full capacity and 2,000 the usual amount. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-7-commentary and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/7-23.html
- **Different units:** Enduring Word on 2 Chronicles 4 quotes the view that Chronicles uses a smaller Babylonian bath. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/
- **Copying error:** Ellicott says Most critics assume this to be correct, meaning the 2,000 in Kings. He himself thinks a "three" probably dropped out of Kings, because two Hebrew words for "thousands" and "two thousand" look the same without vowels. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html
- **Two meanings:** Gill reports the Jewish (Targum) answer: 3,000 dry measure, 2,000 liquid. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/1-kings/7-26.html
- **Spiritual reading:** Bible Hub links the lily rim to the purity the temple required. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/7-26.htm
- **Baptism:** a Restoration Movement commentary says the Sea's size shows the priests washed by immersion, typical of Christian baptism. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/2-chronicles-4.html

**Where Protestant traditions differ:** I found no Lutheran, Methodist, Pentecostal or Anglican writer who disagrees with the others on these verses. The only tradition-linked differences turned up in the Churches of Christ sources: Coffman condemns the oxen as idolatrous images (v. 25), and the Restoration commentary sees immersion baptism in the Sea (v. 26).
